findings.where: Nav bar (the binding strip), the logo lockup at top left, which is also the home link; and the palette, which has no logo colours
findings.fault: Mark's aqueduct mark and the MMM INFRA wordmark are recoloured canary yellow on the maroon strip. The wordmark is set in the page's Caslon, not the logo's Georgia letterforms. This is a reversed version the client does not hold, made without his yes. Logo blue #0070C0 and grey #404040 do not appear anywhere: not in the palette, and not declared logo-only. So the site's one fixed brand asset is the thing that changes.
findings.who_objects: Mark, whose logo the brief says stays and is never redrawn. Also a returning visitor who knows the blue-and-grey mark from his current site, LinkedIn or his documents, and no longer sees it here.

findings.where: First screen at desktop, the 'Write to me' margin note at the far left, outside the double margin line
findings.fault: The page's one action is the lightest item on the first screen. It is small red script parked in the empty left margin, outside the reading column, about 470 px down. The eye goes headline, then photo, then the large aqueduct sketch, and never reaches the margin. In the margin's own red, with a pen stroke under it, it reads as a scribble printed on the pad rather than a way to reach Mark. Visual weight and task priority run in opposite orders.
findings.who_objects: The bank official who has decided to ask Mark about a PPP law. They look for a contact button near his name or photo, find none, and must spot the margin note or fall back on the small 'Contact' link in the nav.

findings.where: Whole page: there is no footer, and the email address is not shown anywhere (the 'Write to me' note is only a mailto link)
findings.fault: Mark's email address never appears as text. The palette names a footer ('Binding: nav, footer'), but the page has none. The page has no contact line at its end and no address a visitor can see or copy.
findings.who_objects: An official at a development bank who works on a managed machine where mailto links open nothing, or who wants to paste the address into a procurement note or forward it to a colleague. They cannot see the address at all.

findings.where: Article specimen, the pull quote 'Whichever PPP Law I am currently working on…'; also the motion sketch title 'written, steady, by hand'
findings.fault: Mark's handwriting font is the signal for the call to action ('one note per view, the call to action in the margin, never body text'). Here it is also used for a static two- to four-line quote and for a panel title. One look now means two things, a link and a quotation, so the hand no longer marks the action. The tile also breaks its own rule.
findings.who_objects: A reader of Mark's article, who sees script on the article page and expects it to be the way to write to him. Also Angélique, who is given a rule ('never body text') that the specimen itself breaks, with no way to know which use is right.

findings.where: Text blocks locked to the 32 px rules: the article heading 'The World's Best Public- / Private Partnership Law' at desktop, the script pull quote (most of all at phone, four widely spaced lines), the motion sketch title at phone, and the small captions under the palette, texture and type pair
findings.fault: Every text block, whatever its size, takes the feints' 32 px step or a multiple of it. A two-line heading is set 64 px apart and splits into two headings at desktop. The script quote at phone falls into separate lines ('on with a client' / 'country!”'). The 15 px captions read double-spaced, like a draft.
findings.who_objects: A reader of an article page (the site's Read mode). A heading or quote that falls apart takes a second look to read as one thought, and every new post Angélique adds will look the same.

findings.where: Article specimen, the lecture row 'Streamlining the PPP Process: Meeting the ‘Abundance’ Challenge'
findings.fault: The title link's underline lands on the pad's feint line on the first line of the title and on the row's dark bottom rule on the last line. It reads as bold text inside a ruled table row, and nothing marks it as a link. On a page where every line of text sits on a rule, an underline is a weak cue, and here it disappears.
findings.who_objects: The visitor looking for Mark's talks, the strongest proof of his judgement on the page. They may not see that the title opens the lecture.

findings.where: Hero, the standalone italic line 'Over 40 years of international infrastructure experience.' (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The first screen gives its own line to a size claim, the weakest kind of standing. It shows no checkable specifics: no regions of work, no kind of mandate, no named body beyond the World Bank line above. The layout makes room for the adjective-style proof and none for the evidence.
findings.who_objects: A procurement-minded official who selects advisers against terms of reference by project kind and region. They discount 'over 40 years' and still don't know whether Mark has worked in their region or sector.

findings.where: The pad itself, at desktop and phone: the feint rules and the double margin line
findings.fault: The palette names blue feints (#93B3D3) and a red margin (#B8322B). Thin and on yellow, they render as dull grey-olive rules and a brownish double line. The marks that make a legal pad read as a legal pad are lost, and the ground reads as plain yellow lined paper.
findings.who_objects: Mark, who asked for a lined yellow legal pad because of his legal background. The pale blue and red lines are what make it recognisably a lawyer's pad.

findings.where: Palette, 'Ballpoint' #1B2A6B against 'Light hand' #34407A, used for the italic asides and dateline
findings.fault: The two inks are near-identical blues given different jobs. As text they cannot be told apart, so the 'asides' role is invisible and looks like a mistake rather than a choice.
findings.who_objects: Few visitors would notice. The layout round and Angélique would carry two text tokens that do the work of one.
